newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: A combination of strong U.S. economic data, switching by investors into stocks and lingering concerns about monetary union wiped one and a half points of French bond futures this week.

After a period of directionless trading close to record highs, bonds suffered from a lack of interest from investors and growing nervousness about the sustainablity of recent gains, pushing 10-year yields up 30 basis points to 5.60 percent.
Growing frustration with a lack of European interest rate cuts, fears of a U.S. rate rise and continued dollar gains left the short end in particularly bad shape on Friday.

Traders said although the March bond future had rebounded after a strong U.S. jobs report, weak hourly earnings being cited as a favourable aspect, the gains had largely been driven by short covering.

After scrambling back close to Thursday's settlement price of 131.26, a U.S. house which had been selling prior to the release of the data once again weighed in to provoke a sharp sell off. The contract continued to decline in GLOBEX trading.
"Everyone went into the number short. No-one can tell me we rose solely on (hourly earnings) after such a solid (jobs) number," a trader at a French bank said.
"It was a classic Friday short squeeze, albeit in disguise, and it doesn't bode well for next week," he said.

The 339,000 rise in the number of non-farm jobs created in the United States in February was higher than the 230,000 rise expected by economists. However some said the slightly lower than expected rise in hourly wages confused the picture and made it less likely the Federal Reserve would raise rates on the basis of this report alone.
Another futures trader said while he expected there to be some weakness at the beginning of next week he thought 130.50 would be a good zone of support.

The short end of the curve came under pressure on Friday. One bond trader at a French bank said a domestic investor had been a large seller of two-year BTANs while another said the sale had been a switch into 10-year French bonds.

Despite the turbulence in the futures market after the U.S. data, the Treasury managed to sell a further 2.05 billion francs of the benchmark 5.5 percent 2007 OAT following Thursday's auction although no new buyers of the 2009 TEC 10 emerged.
The total nominal value of OATs sold this week rose to 26.27 billion, above the Treasury's target of between 23 and 25 billion.

A bond trader said, "Two and three-year paper is an expensive part of the curve and no longer offers protection in the case of a European economic rebound and we're seeing the first signs...There is no fundamental reason to buy it."

"Even if an increase in rates can be ruled out in the coming months, the simply uncertainty about the state of economic growth is sufficient to justify the addition of a risk premium that was no longer there at the short end," he said.
PIBOR contracts suffered along with the front of the yield curve and one PIBOR trader at a U.S. house said there was a good chance the June contract could fall back to 96.50.
For the third day in a row the decline in French long-dated bonds was mirrored by a record close on the French CAC 40 index of blue-chip stocks.

Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris, said, "A large switch in domestic portfolios choices is also playing in favour of the stock market...investors progressively came to our view that there is no more value in the French bond market."
The franc gained ground against the mark to trade at 3.37 while it continued to fall against the dollar, touching a low of 5.8037, down 12 percent since December.
